title: Megalopolis: Differences between the Original Script & The Finished Film

commenti.body:
Thank you for the write-up! It sounds as if a lot of the film’s problems stem from Coppola (1) compromising Cesar Catalina as a credibly human character and (2) shrinking from the full implications of the Cataline conspiracy in favor of forced optimism. What you describe probably still would’ve been a mess, but at least it would’ve had some sense of real stakes. Instead, Coppola turned Catalina into a wish fulfillment fantasy. Defanging the statutory rape plotline is particularly flagrant, and it’s hard not to interpret it as Coppola blowing the raspberry at those who criticized him for harboring Victor Salva. 

I’m also struck that Coppola seems to’ve cannibalized the original ending for *The Godfather Part 3*. I would be curious to know whether he rejected the ending with Julia’s death and Cicero’s despair before or after *Part 3* went into production. (Also, Giancarlo Esposito could’ve acted the hell out of the original ending! What a waste…)

Interesting, thanks for the breakdown. I've read this script, it's more than a quarter century old at this point, I think I read it back in the late 90s or very early 00s when people were circulating paper copies of that, Kevin Smith's Superman, and others.

A lot of the changes, in my view, are because the world is different in 2024 than it was in the 1990s. The original script is much more dated in a lot of ways, especially when it comes to the sexual politics. 

It's really worth looking into various scripts and reading the iterations over the years. And comparing to an eventual film. The shooting script is really interesting as well, comparing (for example) Silence of the Lambs shooting script with the finished movie, you see exactly why those scenes were cut. One of the best examples of a screenplay that gets translated almost verbatim to the screen is Unforgiven. 

I'm also a huge hater of Apocalypse Now Redux, especially the French plantation scene, but if you read some of the earlier drafts, the whole thing is heavy-handed as hell, the French plantation scene is subtle in comparison. Coppola (or maybe mostly Murch and company) made the right decisions.

The other thing I would say about Megaopolis is that the older script would have been harder to film, harder to pull off. A lot of it isn't that visual, it's not clear how that part of the story would be told visually. It makes sense on paper but not sure how it could be filmed to make the points clear. It's almost like there'd need to be a heavy-handed voiceover. There's so much in the action lines that wouldn't be clear at all in a movie, it almost reads more like a novella, like the medium is wrong.

I still haven't watched Redux and I don't know if I ever will, but I did watch the Final Cut a couple of years ago. I liked it but I thought it was touch too long. I found the plantation scene interesting, but felt like I didn't need it. Then earlier this year, I rewatched the theatrical cut and thought it was missing something and wondered if maybe the final cut *is* better.

As a working screenwriter, I’ll attest to the fact that there’s rarely if ever an “original” script as opposed to a shooting script. It’s usually a case of the “original” script being draft 12 and the shooting script being draft 21. You are ALWAYS working and reworking the script. 

Scripts that leak to the public are almost always just “a draft.” Not the original draft. Not the first draft. Not the tenth draft. Not the twentieth draft. A draft. 

Last year a script of mine made the Blacklist (a year end “favorite list” of unproduced screenplays. The script that is out there and that people have read wasn’t even the most recent draft up until that date. 

A normal script, best case scenario, undergoes no shortage of changes before it reaches the screen. A script like Megalopolis, whose concept has existed in some capacity since the late 70s, must have vast sums of drafts over the years. 

Regardless of how someone feels about the end product (my personal suspicion is that Coppola still tried to make a 300 million dollar version on a 100 million dollar budget, and that’s one of the few key reasons it didn’t quite work, even if I thought it had some dazzling stretches, ideas and concepts), it’s an intriguing thing to explore how one draft differs from the shooting draft, but “original” vs “shooting” isn’t an entirely accurate description of how the process of adapting a script into a film.
i've always like the french plantation scene or maybe i just like the idea of it, going 'back in time' in a sense as you go deeper down the river

I think that at  some point in life Coppola stopped being a cynical, disenchanted person (the turning point may have been Tucker, which is very capraesque and optimistic in tone), and started to have a little more faith in humanity.

Hence the massive script rewrite.

> Regardless of how someone feels about the end product (my personal suspicion is that Coppola still tried to make a 300 million dollar version on a 100 million dollar budget, and that’s one of the few key reasons it didn’t quite work, even if I thought it had some dazzling stretches, ideas and concepts),

There are rumors of a finished 4 hour cut of Megalopolis, that at some point Coppola decided to cut because he thought that it subtextually and thematically it was very redundant, and that a lot of the exposition like sequences dragged down the pace (supposedly a lot of them were replaced by psychedelic montages). 

Personally I had  no problems at all following the story (in fact I thought it was quite straightforward), and the main characters arcs were well presented (and closed), but a lot of the subplot elements  came, made their point and then suddenly disappeared. 

Maybe a longer cut could fix this particular issue.

I think the French plantation scene is really interesting and gives a different point of view of why Kurtz is both successfully fighting the Vietcong and why he will ultimately lose.  He's trying to make Vietnam his home and defending his little part of it.  No tour of duty or limited deployments.

> it almost reads more like a novella, like the medium is wrong.

Supposedly the novelization that's (again: supposedly) coming out at some point was based on an earlier version of the script. So it's possible what you said may turn out to be prophetic.
